title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Shipyards | MPI, US
description: Magnetic particle inspection for US shipyards and ports: hull welds, hooks, pad-eyes, shafts and crane steel, mobilized to your yard. Request an MT quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Shipyards, Vessels and Ports
html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection (MPI, also called mag particle testing) on ferritic steel structure in US shipyards, repair yards and port terminals: hull and deck welds, stiffener and bracket connections, rudder and shaft components, crane pedestals, hooks, pad-eyes and rigging fittings. Our technicians travel to your site, whether that is a graving dock, a floating drydock or a pier. To start, request an MT inspection quote and attach the weld list or equipment register.

Why surface cracks matter on a vessel

Fatigue cracks on ships start at the surface, usually at a weld toe, a re-entrant corner or a scar left by a temporary attachment. Once a crack has formed at a stiffener end or a hatch-coaming corner, every wave cycle opens it a little more. MT is the fastest way to find these cracks on carbon and low-alloy steel because the flux leakage they create pulls fine iron particles into a visible line, even when the crack is tight and shallow. It also finds cracks that lie just beneath a thin coating of paint or weld spatter, which is common on a repaired hull.

The method works only on ferromagnetic material. Ordinary hull steel, cast steel, forged shafting and most crane structures qualify. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys and titanium do not, so those parts go to liquid penetrant testing. For flaws below the near-surface zone, or for thickness, the answer is ultrasonic testing.

US requirements behind the work

Commercial vessels fall under the US Coast Guard rules in 46 CFR, and the vessel's classification society sets the rules for materials, welding and survey. The examination method itself follows ASME Section V, Article 7, and the process standards ASTM E709 for the practice and ASTM E1444 for the detailed procedure requirements. Hull welding specifications often reference AWS D3.5. Navy contracts name NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 as the governing nondestructive testing document; we mention it as the controlling document only and make no claim of NAVSEA qualification. Port cranes and lifting gear are generally maintained under the ASME B30 series, and the owner's inspection program calls the interval.

Atlantis technicians are qualified under the company written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician performs and interprets the examination; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. We apply the acceptance criterion in your specification, and the owner or surveyor decides what happens to each indication.

Hull, deck and tank welds

Most shipyard MPI is weld work. Tee welds between plating and stiffeners, bracket toes, bulkhead-to-shell joints, hatch-coaming corners, ballast tank boundary welds and engine-seating plates all concentrate stress and all sit on carbon steel. The technician cleans the surface, applies a suspension or dry powder, magnetizes the part and reads the indications under adequate light. Wet visible particles on a contrast paint work well in daylight on deck; a fluorescent suspension reads better inside a tank or under a tent, provided the area can be darkened enough for ultraviolet light.

Because a flaw is found only when the field crosses it at a useful angle, each area is examined in two directions, usually with an alternating-current yoke whose legs are rotated between passes. Prods give a deeper current path on thick sections but can burn the surface, so most yards restrict or prohibit them on finished welds. We follow the written practice and the specification on which equipment is allowed. Our magnetic particle weld inspection page describes the weld technique across all industries.

Lifting equipment, hooks and port crane parts

A single cracked hook or pad-eye can drop a load over people and cargo. Hooks, shackles, eye plates, lifting lugs, sheave pins and deck-crane pedestals are classic MT candidates, since most of these parts are forged or cast steel. The surface must be cleaned of grease, scale and thick paint, and the technician must reach the high-stress zones: the saddle of a hook, the neck below the shank thread, the weld around a pad-eye and the fillets at a load pin. Equipment that carries a rated load needs a documented inspection record, and MT findings go into that record. Where components have been removed from service, the examination can be done on a bench in the yard or terminal; otherwise it is performed in place with access arranged by the facility. For details specific to this equipment, see magnetic particle inspection of lifting equipment.

Shafting, rudders and repair welds

Propeller shafts, rudder stocks and intermediate shafts are forged steel that carries torque and bending for decades. Fillets at keyways, flange radii and the taper where a propeller seats are places where a fatigue crack can start, and a crack there can end in a lost propeller. MPI on shafting is normally done when the shaft is out or exposed during a drydock period, and the results are recorded for the owner's engineer. Repair welding creates its own need. After a crack is ground out, MT confirms it is gone before the groove is welded; after welding and grinding, MT checks the finished repair. Gouging and carbon-arc work leave hard, brittle zones that can crack hours later, so the final inspection should be scheduled after the part has cooled.

Technique points that decide quality

  • Surface preparation: blast or grind to bright metal at the examination zone; paint, rust and weld spatter hide fine indications or give false ones.
  • Field strength: a yoke must pass a lift test for its rated pull, and a magnetic field indicator or gauge is used to confirm the field direction on complex shapes.
  • Particle type: visible particles for yard-light work, fluorescent for tank interiors and high sensitivity, dry powder for rough surfaces in warm weather.
  • Temperature: a hot deck in summer dries a wet suspension too quickly; a freezing pier thickens it. The procedure states the allowable surface range.
  • Demagnetization: where residual magnetism could affect a compass, shaft bearing or later welding, the part is demagnetized and checked.

Planning around yard schedules and conditions

Shipyard NDT is rarely done in a quiet, clean workshop. A vessel in drydock has trades working on every level: blasters, painters, welders, pipefitters and riggers all want the same hull section. MT needs the surface blasted or ground first and needs a gap before the next coating goes on, so the inspection must be fitted between those steps. Tell us the sequence on the work list and we will say where an examination has to land. Weld repairs on thick or highly restrained joints may carry a hold time before final inspection, set by the specification, and the schedule has to respect it.

Weather and location add variables. Wind scatters dry powder and carries overspray onto a freshly cleaned surface; rain washes a suspension off; cold thickens it. Tents, windbreaks and a stable light source cost far less than a re-inspection. Where the vessel is afloat at a pier, the examination of the lower hull waits for drydock, and above-waterline work such as deck equipment, mooring fittings and hatch coamings can be done earlier. Foreign-flag vessels may bring their own class requirements and a surveyor who attends the work; we support that with a clear indication record at the point of examination.

What the report contains

The MT report names the vessel or structure and each component by frame, drawing or tag number. It states the procedure and revision, the specification and acceptance criterion, the yoke or coil, the particle product and batch, the field verification, the surface condition and the lighting. Each indication is recorded by location, type and length, with a sketch or photograph, and marked accept or reject against the named criterion. The technician and qualification level appear, with the ASNT Level III reviewer. If a surface was not accessible, the report lists it as not examined instead of leaving it out.

What to send for a quote

  • Vessel or facility, location and the dates the yard or terminal can give us
  • Weld list, drawings or equipment register, with quantities and sizes
  • Material grades, coating system and whether coatings come off
  • The specification, class rule or NAVSEA requirement that applies
  • Access, scaffolding, power supply, confined-space and TWIC arrangements

Where we work in the US marine market

We mobilize to yards, piers and terminals across the coasts and rivers. These pages cover MT by port city.

  • Norfolk: ship repair and Navy maintenance with constant weld repair.
  • Pascagoula: Gulf Coast shipbuilding and heavy fabrication.
  • Mobile: shipyard and offshore vessel work on Mobile Bay.
  • San Diego: Pacific repair yards and pier-side work.
  • Seattle: ferries, fishing vessels and Puget Sound drydocks.
  • New Orleans: river terminals, barge fleets and shore cranes.
  • Baltimore: Chesapeake yards and bulk handling terminals.
  • Charleston: container cranes and port steel.

Training your own technicians

A yard that runs its own MT needs people qualified under a written practice. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training aligned to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, practice on the magnetic particle simulator, and procedure support through our NDT procedure development service. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A. Marine employers can also review maritime NDT training. For the method in general, see the national magnetic particle testing page.

What we do not do here

Radiography is outside what Atlantis can perform in the United States, and specialist techniques are not part of this page. MT is limited to magnetic material and to flaws that reach or lie close to the surface. We do not issue class certificates or act as class surveyor. Class-credited ship thickness work is a separate matter, covered on our maritime page, where Atlantis is in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be used on stainless or aluminum parts of a ship?
faq.a: No. MT needs a ferromagnetic material, so austenitic stainless, aluminum and copper alloys are examined by liquid penetrant testing instead. Duplex stainless grades vary, so the procedure confirms the response first.

faq.q: Can you test through paint on a hull weld?
faq.a: Thin, tightly bonded coatings can be examined, but the procedure sets a maximum thickness and requires a demonstration that known indications still show. Loose, thick or damaged coatings must come off at the examination zone.

faq.q: What is the difference between MPI and mag particle testing?
faq.a: Nothing in practice. MPI, MT and mag particle testing all describe the same method: magnetize the steel, apply iron particles and look for a line where flux leaks at a surface flaw.

faq.q: Do you inspect crane hooks and rigging fittings in a port?
faq.a: Yes, on the steel parts. We examine hooks, shackles, pad-eyes, lugs and pins to the owner's inspection program and record the result in the equipment record. Rated-load decisions stay with the owner's competent person.

faq.q: Who decides if an indication on a weld is acceptable?
faq.a: The acceptance criterion comes from your specification or class rule. Our Level II technician records and classifies each indication against it, and the owner, yard quality department or surveyor decides on repair or acceptance.

faq.q: Is a yoke enough, or do you need other equipment?
faq.a: A yoke covers most weld and fitting work on hulls and decks. Coils or a central conductor are used on shafts and round parts when the specification calls for them, and the written practice defines what is permitted.

faq.q: Can MT be done in a ballast tank?
faq.a: Yes, with a confined-space permit, ventilation and rescue arrangements from the vessel or yard. Fluorescent particles work well inside tanks when the area can be darkened, and electrical equipment must suit the atmosphere.

faq.q: Is radiography on ship welds available through Atlantis in the US?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. For volume examination of ship welds we offer ultrasonic testing where the code and the owner accept it.

faq.q: How should we sequence MT with blasting and painting in a drydock period?
faq.a: Plan the examination after surface preparation and before the final coating, and after any hold time that the weld specification requires. Share the work sequence with us at quoting so the inspection window is built into the schedule.
